title: Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36–46)
hook: he asks the cup to pass, then not my will but thine; they fall asleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, the basin and towel, the Mandatum: at the last supper he knelt and washed their feet. Your line was as I have done to you. What small, humble thing did you do for someone? Day sixty-one.

Supper is over. They sing a hymn, and they walk out of the city in the dark, down across a little valley and up into an olive grove on the far side. He tells most of them to sit and wait while he goes on to pray, and takes three with him: Peter, James and John. Then, Matthew says, he begins to grow sorrowful and to be sad, and he tells them so. In the Douay-Rheims: "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." The one who calmed storms is asking his friends not to leave him alone. Then he goes a few steps further, falls on his face, and prays. Today's word is the name of that garden.
screen: `OUT OF THE CITY, IN THE DARK.` → `PETER, JAMES AND JOHN.` → `STAY YOU HERE, AND WATCH WITH ME.`

segments.voice: The name Gethsemane most likely comes from Aramaic words for an oil press, a place where olives were crushed until the oil ran out. Matthew never stops to explain the name. He goes straight to the prayer: "My Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me. Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The chalice, the cup, is an old biblical picture for what life pours out for you to drink, and here it means the suffering coming at dawn. Notice he asks. He doesn't pretend he wants it. Luke even says his sweat fell like drops of blood. The Church teaches that Jesus had a real human will, and this is where you can hear it: a man who does not want to die, handing himself over anyway. Luke puts it in the words of today's line, in the Douay-Rheims: "not my will, but thine be done." Then he walks back, and the three are asleep. "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" He isn't furious. He almost makes excuses for them: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh weak." Three times he prays. Three times they sleep. Catholics keep that hour. On the night of Holy Thursday, after the evening Mass, the Blessed Sacrament is carried to a side altar, and people come to watch with him into the night. Tradition ties the holy hour, an hour of prayer before the Eucharist, to that same question.
screen: `AN OIL PRESS, WHERE OLIVES ARE CRUSHED.` · `LET THIS CHALICE PASS FROM ME.` · `A REAL HUMAN WILL, HANDED OVER.` · `COULD YOU NOT WATCH ONE HOUR?` · then, large: `NOT MY WILL, BUT THINE BE DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay awake with someone's pain. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is carrying something heavy right now: an illness, a loss, a fear. You can't fix it. That's not the job tonight. The job is only to stay. Hold them in your mind and don't drift off to your own list. When you notice you've wandered, come back, the way he came back to his sleeping friends. If you pray, you can simply pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Gethsemane. The olive grove across the valley, whose name probably means oil press, where he prayed and his friends slept. Today's word.
Your line: not my will. Today, when something doesn't go your way, say the whole thing honestly first, the way he did, and then see if you can let it go. Day sixty-one.

howItsDone: On Holy Thursday night Catholic parishes keep the Blessed Sacrament at an altar of repose so people can watch and pray with Jesus, and some Catholics keep a regular holy hour before the Eucharist.

original.note: Greek spelling of a name most likely from Aramaic words for an oil press.

trapdoor: what you thought: a garden where Jesus prayed before he was arrested.
what it means: a man who does not want to suffer says so, then hands his will over to his Father while his friends sleep.
what a scholar hears: gat shemanim, an oil press in an olive grove. the Church reads this prayer as the human will of Jesus freely joining the Father's.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Matthew 26:38–41 given from memory; confirm punctuation and exact words (e.g. 'the flesh weak').
Luke 22:42 in the Douay-Rheims: the teach paraphrases it as 'not my will, but thine be done' without quotation marks; confirm and quote if desired.
Gethsemane from Aramaic gat shemanim ('oil press'): the common derivation; stated as 'most likely'. Confirm the Greek spelling Γεθσημανί.
Luke 22:43–44 (the angel and the sweat like drops of blood) is absent from some early manuscripts; the script says only 'Luke even says'. Keeper may want a note.
Human will of Jesus: Third Council of Constantinople (681); CCC 612 on the agony. Confirm the reference.
Holy Thursday altar of repose and the holy hour described in general terms; confirm.
